newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity top brass on offensive with meetings.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity top brass on offensive with meetings.

text.p: Fidelity Investments' top brass, armed with a new deal with Salomon Brothers and sweeping changes among its mutual fund managers, went on the offensive Tuesday with the first of six meetings with its top clients.

Stung by negative press over the past year and a dwindling share of new assets, Fidelity took its case directly to its most senior clients with closed-door meetings at New York's Waldorf-Astoria Hotel on Tuesday.

Last week, the mutual fund giant announced a deal with Salomon Brothers to offer its discount brokerage customers up to 10 percent of any intial public or secondary offerings in which Salomon is the lead manager, a Salomon spokeswoman said.
Also under the deal, Fidelity will give its customers access to Salomon's stock research, a step up from Fidelity's limited RealTime Research Package.

The Salomon deal and plans to boost its Funds Network mutual fund supermarket is seen as a move to counter Charles Schwab & Co. Inc.'s discount brokerage and its popular OneSource Web site, analsyts said.

In a move against the Vanguard Group, whose index funds took market share from Fidelity last year, Fidelity plans to add more index funds this year in addition to its three stock funds which track the S&P 500 and its one bond index fund.

For the first time, Vanguard took in more new cash in its mutual funds than Fidelity did in 1996, fund analysts said. The $32.5 billion Vanguard Index 500 Portfolio, which tracks the S&P 500, beat all but five of Fidelity's U.S. diversified stock funds in 1996, analsyts said.

"A billion dollars a week has been coming into index funds, and that's Vanguard and others, and they (Fidelity) want to make sure they get a piece of that," said Don Dion, publisher of Fidelity Independent Advisor, a newsletter which follows Fidelity funds.
Fidelity also plans to cut fees on its bond mutual funds, and over the last year has made extensive changes in the management of its stock funds following the departure of many portfolio managers.

"They've recognised a lot of the stuff that has happened in the past year, and they've taken a more defensive tack to the issue," said Eric Kobren, editor of Fidelity Insight, which closely follows the company.

Dion said he expects the executives to tell their customers the fund company still has a solid portfolio management team despite the defections and that the funds are sticking to their investment objectives after a disastrous 1996 for some of them. They may also outline steps to keep managers from leaving, he said.
"They are clearly on the offensive, they have sort of come out of their shell," Dion said, noting that many of the executives are making themselves more available to the press.
After the all-day meeting in New York, Fidelity will open a session for retail customers to the press Tuesday evening.
Following the New York meeting, the executives will go to Atlanta on Wednesday, then on to Dallas, San Francisco and Chicago, ending in Boston on Jan. 30, Fidelity said.
